Exploring the value of CO2 shipping transport flexibility in international batchwise transportation
                             carbon capture and storage networks

               Denis Martins Fragaa*, Anna Korrea,b, Zhenggang Niea, Şevket Durucana
     a

Abstract

The benefits of CO₂ shipping transport within international Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) networks have been
growing in importance as it offers flexibility and allows to postpone investment in capital-intensive infrastructure until
enough CCS projects are launched. This work explores this value through a comparative cost assessment of 15 what-
if scenarios devised for standalone and integrated CCS networks, designed around the Northern Lights project and the
UK's Teesside cluster. The analysis is performed by implementing a Multi-period, Multi-mode, and Multi-objective
Mixed integer linear programming (MoMilp) model developed at Imperial College London and considering all the
elements of the CCS value chain after CO2 is captured (i.e. conditioning, intermediate storage and injection in the
saline aquifer), allowing to account for individual regional characteristics in terms of design and network costs. The
configurations of the different scenarios are used to analyse the implications of CCS network development hold up,
e.g. for a part of the network to become available at a later period, or for the CO2 emission growth to occur at a later
time in the planning horizon. The simulation results illustrate the interplay between postponing CCS network
infrastructure investment and generating gains of scale in an existing network. This flexibility between CCS networks
could provide relevant cost reduction while maximising the storage of CO2.

Keywords: Batchwise transportation; Carbon Capture and storage (CCS) networks; CCS network integration



1. Introduction

   The importance of carbon capture and storage (CCS) in Europe is growing, with a 61% increase in commercial-
scale projects, reaching 119 projects in 2023. The main driver for this growth is the support secured from the European
Commission and national governments, including funding mechanisms (i.e. Innovation Fund, Horizon Europe, and
Cluster Sequencing in the UK), large-scale development plans (e.g., Green Deal Industrial Plan) and legislative support
from both the European Commission and the UK [1, 2]. The increasing maturity of these projects starts shaping the
infrastructure available for storing increasing amounts of CO2, helping countries achieve their decarbonisation targets.
   The most advanced project (i.e. Northern Lights) is characterised by batchwise transportation, facilitated by CO2
transport ships, and injection via a relatively short pipeline to storage formations in the Norwegian North Sea. The
transport infrastructure is supported by two intermediate storage hubs that aim to help manage and assure the flow in
the network. Multiple other opportunities are being studied in different regions to test multi-mode transportation
options. However, such efforts are at different stages of maturity and are often developed considering an optimum

    This work analyses and presents the value of batchwise CCS transport networks' flexibility by performing
comparative cost assessments of standalone CCS networks with scenarios identified to serve what-if analysis and to
assess the benefits of integrated CCS network design. The what-if analysis conceptualisation is applied for batchwise
CCS network analogues of the Nothern Lights project (NL), the Stella Maris concept (SM), and the Teesside cluster
in the UK, as this is the most advanced track-1 project.

2. Methodology

   The approach follows the 4-step methodology described in Fig. 1. The first step consists of the cost data gathering
and the bottom-up cost design. For the batch-wise infrastructure (e.g., vessels, intermediate storage and conditioning),
the costs are sourced from existing models developed by the authors [3,4,5] and account for the regional cost
differences between the networks, considering ships with 6, 20, and 50 CO2 kt CO2 capacity, three onshore (i.e. 6",
12", 18") and offshore (i.e. 36", 40", 48") pipeline diameters.

3. Implementation in the case study

    Initially, the models were run in three cases comprising a standalone version of the UK and NL+SM networks and
an integrated (UK+NL+SM) scenario to set up the base cases (i.e. 0, 1, 2 cases) to be compared against the what-if
scenarios. Fig. 2 illustrates the boundary of these networks, their routing for batchwise and offshore pipeline transport
options, and the stationary emitters considered within each. The UK concept is assumed to be formed by the Net Zero
Teesside (NTZ) and Solent area stationary emitters, representing a cluster of individual stationary emitters connected
to their intermediate storage Hub (Teesside hub and Solent Hub). The NL+SM concept combines individual stationary
emitters and clusters of emitters. The stationary emitters from NL are Yara (1), a fertiliser plant at Herøya in
Porsgrunn, Fortum Oslo Varme -FOV (3), a waste incineration plant in Klemetsrud, near Oslo, Preem (4), a refinery
in Lysekil, Sweden.

4. Results

    The 15 what-if scenarios are systematically evaluated against their corresponding base case to evaluate the
batchwise transport opportunity in terms of key metrics, namely total cost, unit cost, levelised cost (i.e. discounted at
10%), emission profile, ship fleet size, ship trips per year, and the accumulated quantity of wells in the network. Table
2 summarises the results and compares the cost metrics of all scenarios relative to the respective base case.
Summarising the results for all scenarios against their respective base case, the yearly percentage change in CO2
emission varied by ±62%, resulting in a yearly variation of total optimal cost ranging from -71% to 316%, a yearly
ship fleet (i.e., considering all ship capacities) variation from -3 to 5 ships, and yearly trips variation from -212 to 343
trips. A comparison throughout the the 30-year time horizon for the network design metrics (i.e. emission profile, total
cost, and batchwise network) for each scenario is presented in the appendix. Furthermore, Fig. 4. illustrates the cost
metrics across all cases and scenarios and a cross-scenario heat map with the variance against their respective base
case.

5. Conclusions

    This study has developed and analysed three distinct batchwise CCS network cases — standalone and integrated
— and a total of 15 what-if scenarios designed to assess the value that CO2 shipping flexibility can offer in evolving
CCS networks. The integrated scenario encompassing the UK, Northern Lights (NL), and Stella Maris (SM) concepts
demonstrated reduced variability across all cost metrics analysed, including total cost, levelised cost, and unit cost, as
compared to the standalone configuration across most cases for the design parameters adopted in the analysis. These
results indicate the positive economic advantages of a coordinated CCS network infrastructure.
    Moreover, the integrated UK+NL+SM scenario achieved a lower optimal ship fleet size, suggesting that fleet
sharing and trip optimisation can be viable strategies for reducing operational costs and improving logistical efficiency
(i.e. base cases). Allowing the interconnection (i.e. SM to the UK) marginally lowered the cost metrics, indicating
potential synergies from ship trips. The opposite, i.e. considering that the UK may direct CO2 towards NL after 10
years, has not changed the network configuration, indicating that once storage sites become operational, with the
relevant infrastructure in place (i.e. offshore pipelines), the cost differentials between storage sites must be material to
change the economics and divert the CO2 flow.
